title: Inishrush, Dunaghy & Drumragh collateral leads
standfirst: Family-register, census, tithe and marriage evidence places several Glasgow-associated households around Inishrush. The records illuminate a neighbourhood and possible collateral paths, not a joined Lisnagaver pedigree.
question: Can Inishrush, Dunaghy and Drumragh records establish a documented bridge to the later Rasharkin households?
answer: John born in 1767 is probably the 1831 Inishrush householder, but no Irish record names his parents. Adam, born about 1758, cannot be his father; brotherhood or cousinship remains possible. A later marriage makes the James in John’s 1847 letter a strong identification, while still not proving that younger Adam was Adam Glasgow-3902 or that this group was kin to Lisnagaver. Adam and older Alexander now share a selected uncertain Larne father in the local model; this does not establish the 1767 John’s kinship or identify the younger Adam.

chapters.title: Larne and Inishrush: James’s possible sons Adam and Alexander
body: Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other.

A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The two local 1740 Tamlaght Hugh households, including Glasgow-3931, and the older Adam-and-Maria naming model remain alternatives for Adam. A different unrecorded father remains possible. Neither Larne property succession nor the Inishrush household totals connect these generations. The 1831 return does not identify its unnamed occupants, and the later plot-29 succession is not evidence of James the ropemaker’s paternity. The shared [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) field is a recently created research placeholder, not evidence that Adam, older Alexander and Glasgow-1367 were brothers. It is not identified or merged with James. No father is extended to Glasgow-1367, and no unnamed extra generation is added.

Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. The 2007 account and its copied 2020 restatement are one source tradition, not independent witnesses. Daniel and Thomas are proved brothers, but their father’s name is not established by a contemporary parent record. The new James father therefore depends on that reconstructed older Alexander account. Younger Glasgow-951 remains a separate, unresolved possible brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel; the record-defined Glasgow-4090 remains his leading current father comparison. This batch does not select older Alexander as younger Alexander’s father or place that younger family beneath James. No Rosanna surname or October 1822 death date is newly established. James’s own Glasgow-1505 and Glasgow-1499 ancestry alternatives and existing children retain their earlier assessments.

Two named father hypotheses are selected from existing research, with low/very low confidence. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. All existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics remain unchanged. Mothers are independently unassigned. The local model replaces the placeholder father only in these two selected views; captured WikiTree fields and rival parentage remain available. Counts describe retained profile accounts and conditional ancestry, not a proved pedigree.

evidence.label: Tamlaght gravestone: Adam died 30 June 1844 aged 86; Rose died 31 July 1833 aged 66; photograph and transcription
Registry of Deeds, ropewalk lease 10 September 1760, registered 24 November 1763: Belfast ropemaker taking Gardenmore, Larne
Registry of Deeds, assignment 28 March 1768: matching Larne ropewalk and lease term
Registry memorial 204122, 14 May 1766: James Glasgow, Larne ropemaker, witness
Registry affidavit sworn 27 October 1773, registered 15 November: Larne gentleman aged upwards of thirty
Genes Reunited thread 465937: 2007 descendant account, later copied; previously reviewed derivative testimony, not contemporary proof
1740 Protestant Householders’ Return, Macafee transcription: two Tamlaght Hugh households, no stated kinship

chapters.title: John, Mary and the Inishrush household
body: John and Mary Arthur’s family Bible records their 1798 marriage and nine children. The close fit between that family and the 1831 Inishrush house makes the repeated identity probable, not certain.
The Bible is strong family evidence but does not name John's parents. Its naming pattern makes older Adam and Maria useful search names only.

chapters.title: A letter points to a later marriage
body: John's 1847 letter relayed that James Glasgow had a child by a servant who was Henry Barkly's daughter. The 1851 marriage of James, farmer of Inishrush and son of Adam, to Rosanna Barkley of Tyanee closely matches those particulars.
The child is unnamed, and this does not establish that James's father was Adam Glasgow-3902.

chapters.title: Dunaghy, Drumragh and Rasharkin
body: The 1825 tithe list records Robert Glasco at Dunbught and two distinct James Glasgows at Ballybogey; 'junior' alone does not prove father and son. A 1828 marriage identifies Mary Glasgow of Drumragh in the wider area.
Maria Glasgow's documented Wallace children were born at Rasharkin in 1840 and 1842. That places one Inishrush descendant branch beside Lisnagaver, without proving kinship.

clusters.title: John and Mary Arthur
clusters.summary: Bible, locality and household evidence strongly support John-822 as the Inishrush-associated John.
clusters.boundary: No record names his parents; the pending duplicate identity is not a proved merge.

clusters.title: James and the Barkley connection
clusters.summary: The 1851 marriage closely fits the James and Barkley details in John’s 1847 letter.
clusters.boundary: It does not identify the unnamed child or prove older Adam's identity.

clusters.title: Neighbouring collateral occurrences
clusters.summary: Tithe and marriage records identify several named local occurrences and a Rasharkin descendant movement.
clusters.boundary: They do not establish links among the households or to Lisnagaver.
